title: The town that struck water instead of oil
lede: Beverly Hills began as a failed oil play. The investors who drilled the old Rancho Rodeo de las Aguas found water instead, so they built a town around it, a hotel to sell it, and curving streets each lined with its own kind of tree. Then the movie stars arrived, voted to stay independent, and turned about 5.7 square miles into the most famous ZIP code in the world.

ch.h: An oil company that found a town
fact: residents when the city incorporated in 1914
p: Before it had a name, this was Rancho Rodeo de las Aguas, the gathering of the waters, where streams draining Benedict, Coldwater and Franklin canyons met near today's Sunset Boulevard and Beverly Drive. In 1900 a group of oilmen including Burton Green bought the land, drilled, and came up mostly with water. In 1906 they reorganized as the Rodeo Land and Water Company, named the place after Beverly Farms, Massachusetts, and started selling lots instead of oil.

Green hired landscape architect Wilbur Cook to make it a garden city: curving streets north of Santa Monica Boulevard, a long park along the boulevard, and different street trees on different streets so blocks have their own canopy. To bring in buyers, the company built the Beverly Hills Hotel in 1912 on the spot where the waters met. It worked. By 1914 there were enough residents to incorporate, about 550 of them.

ch.h: The stars who kept Beverly Hills independent
fact: film stars who campaigned against annexation
p: In 1919 Mary Pickford and Douglas Fairbanks, then the most famous couple in the world, bought a hunting lodge on Summit Drive and had it remade into Pickfair. Other stars followed them up the hill, and Beverly Hills became the place Hollywood went home to at night.

By 1923 the town was running short of water, and joining Los Angeles looked like the fix. Pickford, Fairbanks, Will Rogers, Rudolph Valentino, Harold Lloyd, Tom Mix, Conrad Nagel and Fred Niblo campaigned against it door to door. Supporters of annexation answered by leaving bottles of the local sulfur-smelling water on doorsteps. On April 24, 1923, voters chose independence anyway. Rogers was named honorary mayor in 1926, and the eight stars are honored today by the Celluloid Monument.

fact: acres of Doheny Ranch that became Trousdale
p: Oilman Edward L. Doheny owned the hills above the flats. In 1928 the family completed Greystone, a Tudor Revival mansion of about 46,000 square feet designed by Gordon Kaufmann as a gift for his son. When a later owner planned to tear it down, the city bought the estate in 1965, and in 1971 its gardens opened as a public park. It is still one of the most filmed houses in Los Angeles.

In 1954 builder Paul Trousdale bought about 410 acres of the Doheny Ranch, persuaded Beverly Hills to bring it into the city, and laid out roughly 530 terraced lots with an architectural committee approving every house. Architects including Paul R. Williams, Wallace Neff and A. Quincy Jones designed low, glassy homes oriented to the views, and Trousdale became the mid-century address of Elvis Presley, Frank Sinatra, Dean Martin, Ray Charles and Richard Nixon. City rules still limit building height on most lots to protect those views.

ch.h: From a farm town to the Golden Triangle
fact: the year the hotel got its script logo
p: South of Santa Monica Boulevard, Cook's grid became the business district now called the Golden Triangle. Rodeo Drive took its modern shape in the 1960s and 1970s as designer boutiques replaced neighborhood shops, and Two Rodeo, a cobbled European-style lane at Wilshire, opened in 1990.

The Beverly Hills Hotel was painted pink in 1948, and the next year architect Paul R. Williams added the Crescent Wing and drew the script logo that is still on the sign. He also reshaped the Polo Lounge and the Fountain Coffee Room. More than a century after it opened, the hotel is still the social center the founders built it to be.

dyk: Why is it called Beverly Hills?
Burton Green named it after Beverly Farms, Massachusetts, a seaside town he remembered fondly. The Hills part described the land.
How did the town get started?
Oil investors drilled the old rancho in 1900 and found water instead, so they sold homes rather than oil.
How close did Beverly Hills come to joining LA?
In 1923 voters were asked to annex to Los Angeles for its water. A campaign led by eight movie stars helped defeat it on April 24, 1923.
Why do so many streets look different from each other?
Planner Wilbur Cook gave different streets different trees, so many blocks have their own signature canopy.
Who drew the Beverly Hills Hotel's famous script logo?
Architect Paul R. Williams, who also designed the Crescent Wing in 1949.
